tasks.q: Print whether the first number is greater than the second.
brief: The user types in two whole numbers, one on each line.
Print True if the first is greater than the second, otherwise False.
tasks.starter: # Read two numbers and print True or False

tests.why: 34 is greater than 19, so the comparison is True.
The order matters. True here means the two were compared the wrong way round.
Equal is not greater. This is the test that tells > apart from >=.

tasks.fb: A comparison is already True or False, so you can print it straight out without an if.

teach.say: A comparison is already True or False, so it can be printed straight out. Equal values are not greater.

tasks.q: Print three comparisons of two numbers, one on each line.
brief: The user types in two whole numbers, one on each line.
Print whether they are equal, then whether the first is less than the second.
Then print whether the first is greater than or equal to the second. Three lines in all.
tasks.starter: # Read two numbers, then print the three comparisons

tests.why: 4 is not equal to 9, it is less than 9, and it is not greater than or equal to 9.
Two equal numbers. A False on line 1 means = was used instead of ==, and on line 3 that > was used instead of >=.
Check the three lines come out in the order the brief asks for.

tasks.fb: == asks a question and = stores a value. The two are easy to mix up.

teach.say: == asks whether two values are the same; = stores a value. The rest are < > <= >= and != for not equal.

tasks.q: Print recorded, and a frost warning if it is below zero.
brief: The user types in one whole number: the temperature in Celsius.
Always print exactly: recorded
Then, only when the temperature is below 0, print exactly: frost warning
tasks.starter: # Read the temperature, print recorded, add a warning if needed

tests.why: Below freezing, so both lines print and recorded comes first.
Above freezing. An extra frost warning here means the print is not indented inside the if.
Exactly 0 is not below 0. A warning here means <= was used where the brief says below.

tasks.fb: An if on its own is allowed. You only need an else when something has to happen in the other case.

teach.say: An if runs the indented lines only when its question is True. When it is False nothing happens, and no else is needed.

tasks.q: Say whether a lift load of up to 450 kg may go.
brief: The user types in one whole number: the load in kilograms.
If the load is 450 or less, print exactly: safe to go
Otherwise print exactly: too heavy
tasks.starter: # Read the load and decide whether the lift may go

tests.why: Well inside the limit.
450 or less includes 450 itself. too heavy here means < was used instead of <=.
One kilogram over. safe to go here means the comparison lets too much through.
An empty lift is still a valid load, so it must not fall through to the else.

tasks.fb: 450 or less means <= 450. Always test the exact boundary, because that is where < and <= differ.

teach.say: else catches every case the if did not. Mind the boundary: 7 or less means <= 7, so 7 itself still counts.

tasks.q: Say whether a reservoir level is rising, falling or steady.
brief: The user types in one whole number: the change in level since last week.
Above 0: print exactly rising. Below 0: print exactly falling.
Exactly 0: print exactly steady. One word only, whichever it is.
tasks.starter: # Read the change in level and describe it

tests.why: A positive change means the level went up.
A negative change. rising here means the number was tested rather than compared with 0.
Exactly 0 is the third case, and the one most often forgotten: it belongs to neither > 0 nor < 0.
A large fall still prints one word only, so the branches must not run one after another.

tasks.fb: elif means only ask this if the question above was False, which is why the three branches cannot both run.

teach.say: elif is only asked when the if above it was False, so two branches can never both run. Here neither was True and nothing printed at all, which is what else is for.

tasks.q: Print which postage band a package falls in.
brief: The user types in one whole number: the weight in grams.
100 or less: print exactly letter. Over 100 but 750 or less: print exactly large letter.
Heavier than 750: print exactly parcel. One line only, whichever it is.
tasks.starter: # Read the weight in grams and print its band

tests.why: Inside the lightest band.
Exactly 100 belongs to the first band, because it says 100 or less.
One gram over 100 moves it up a band. letter here means the first test is too generous.
The top of a band belongs to it. parcel here means < 750 was used instead of <= 750.
Anything over 750 falls through to the else.

tasks.fb: Write the bands in order from lightest upwards, and each elif only needs the top of its own band.

teach.say: Each elif only needs the top of its own band, because everything smaller was already dealt with above it.

tasks.q: Say whether a drone may fly, from wind speed and visibility.
brief: The user types in two lines: the wind speed in mph, then the visibility in km.
If the wind is under 20 and the visibility is 5 or more, print exactly: clear to fly
Otherwise print exactly: grounded
tasks.starter: # Read the wind speed and the visibility, then decide

tests.why: Both conditions are met, which is what and requires.
Exactly 20 is not under 20. clear to fly here means <= 20 was used.
Exactly 5 km counts as 5 or more, so this one must pass.
The wind is fine but the visibility is not. With and, one failing side is enough, so this passing means or was used.
Here the visibility is fine and the wind is not, so the other half of the and does the work.

tasks.fb: and needs both sides True, and each side needs its own comparison: wind < 20 and vis >= 5.

teach.say: and is True only when both sides are True. Each side needs its own complete comparison.

tasks.q: Decide whether the door opens, from a staff number and the alarm.
brief: The user types in two lines: a staff number, then the word yes or no for the alarm.
If the number is 7 or 9 and the alarm is not yes, print exactly: open
Otherwise print exactly: locked
tasks.starter: # Read the staff number and the alarm, then decide

tests.why: An allowed staff number with the alarm off.
The second allowed number must work too. locked here means the or checked only one of them.
Not an allowed number. If this opened, the or may be written n == 7 or 9, which Python always treats as True.
The number is allowed but the alarm is set, and not turns that into a refusal.
The alarm beats everything, so its check is joined on with and, not or.

tasks.fb: Each or needs a full comparison on both sides, and brackets round the or keep it from being swallowed by the and.

teach.say: or is True when either side is True, and each side needs its own comparison. not flips True and False over.

tasks.q: Announce the fixture from the weather and the number of players.
brief: The user types in two lines: the word dry or wet, then a whole number of available players.
If dry: print exactly match on for 11 or more players, otherwise exactly friendly instead.
If wet: print exactly indoor training for 11 or more players, otherwise exactly cancelled.
tasks.starter: # Read the weather and the players, then announce the decision

tests.why: Dry with a full side, so the outer if and the inner if are both True.
Exactly 11 is enough, because the rule says 11 or more. friendly instead here means > 11 was used.
Dry but short of players, so the inner else runs while the outer if is still True.
Enough players, but the weather sends it down the other branch.
Both conditions fail, which is the inner else of the outer else.

tasks.fb: The weather chooses which pair of answers you pick from, and the players choose which of that pair you print.

teach.say: An if inside another if is only reached when the outer one was True, so the outer question decides which pair of answers you choose between.

tasks.q: Say where a delivery goes, from its box size and weight.
brief: The user types in two lines: the word small or large, then a whole number of kilograms.
Small box: print exactly locker A for 5 kg or less, otherwise exactly counter.
Large box: print exactly counter for 25 kg or less, otherwise exactly too heavy.
tasks.starter: # Read the box size and the weight, then print where it goes

tests.why: A light small box.
Exactly 5 is 5 or less, so it still goes to the locker.
A small box over 5 kg has only one other place to go, so no weight is too heavy for it.
The same weight goes somewhere else because the size is different. locker A here means the size is not being checked.
Exactly 25 is still allowed at the counter. too heavy here means < 25 was used.
Only a large box can be too heavy, so this answer sits inside the large branch.

tasks.fb: Each size has its own pair of answers, so the weight check belongs inside the branch that tested the size.

teach.say: Comparing words uses == and the spelling has to match exactly. The size chooses which pair of answers you are picking from, and the weight chooses which of the pair.

tasks.q: Work out the medal from three judges' scores.
brief: The user types in three whole numbers out of 10, one on each line.
Check these rules in order and print only the words from the first rule that matches.
All three 9 or more: gold. Total 24 or more: silver. Total 18 or more: bronze. Otherwise: no medal.
tasks.starter: # Read three scores and work out the medal

tests.why: Every score is 9 or more, so the first rule wins.
Exactly 9 counts as 9 or more. silver here means > 9 was used somewhere in the and.
Not all three reach 9, so gold is out, but the total of 26 earns silver.
A total of exactly 24 is 24 or more. bronze here means > 24 was used.
A total of 23 is short of silver but comfortably past 18.
The total is exactly 18, and 18 or more includes it. no medal here means > 18 was used.
A total of 17 is one short, so nothing matches and the else runs.
Low scores all round, which is the plain else at the bottom of the chain.

tasks.fb: Keep the rules in the brief's order, because an earlier branch wins even when a later one would also be True.

teach.say: Both of these are True, so the order of your branches decides the answer: the first True branch wins and the rest are skipped.

tasks.q: With wind 15, visibility 8 and the alarm off, is each condition True or False?
tasks.fb: Work each side out on its own first, then join them with and, or or not.

info.title: One = or two
info.text: A single = stores a value and == compares two. Mixing them up is one of the first bugs every programmer meets.

info.title: No switch here
info.text: Some languages have a switch statement for choosing between many options. Python does the same job with elif.

info.title: Unreachable code
info.text: If a band that catches everything is tested first, no branch below it can ever run - those lines are unreachable.

info.title: Same as the gates
info.text: and, or and not behave exactly like the AND, OR and NOT gates you draw truth tables for in topic 2.4.

info.title: Flatten it
info.text: A nested if can often be replaced by one condition joined with and, which is easier to read and easier to test.

info.title: Read the wording
info.text: 'At least', 'no more than' and 'over' all mean different things. Write the boundary value down before you code it.
